lesson.title: Constant Amount vs. Constant Percent: Linear or Exponential?
lesson.summary: Linear growth adds the same fixed amount every period while exponential growth multiplies by the same factor every period, and even a slower-looking exponential pattern eventually overtakes any linear pattern for good.
lesson.body:
A linear function grows by adding a constant amount each period. That is the constant rate of change you already know from slope, and it produces a straight-line graph. An exponential function grows, or decays, by multiplying by a constant factor each period, which produces a curved graph. The core distinction to hold onto is simple: linear means "add the same number every time," exponential means "multiply by the same number every time."

Here is a worked comparison. Two companies both start an employee at a 40,000 dollar salary. Company A gives a flat raise of 2,000 dollars every year, a linear model: y equals 40,000 plus 2,000 t. Company B gives a 4 percent raise every year, an exponential model with growth factor 1.04 from the earlier chapter: y equals 40,000 times 1.04 raised to the t. Tracking both salaries year by year:

Year 0: Company A is 40,000 dollars, Company B is 40,000 dollars.
Year 1: Company A is 42,000 dollars, Company B is 41,600 dollars.
Year 2: Company A is 44,000 dollars, Company B is 43,264 dollars.
Year 3: Company A is 46,000 dollars, Company B is 44,995 dollars.
Year 4: Company A is 48,000 dollars, Company B is 46,794 dollars.
Year 5: Company A is 50,000 dollars, Company B is 48,666 dollars.

For these first five years, the steady 2,000 dollar raise from Company A pays more than the 4 percent raise from Company B. It would be easy to conclude the flat raise is simply the better deal. But does that hold forever? No. Because the 4 percent is applied to an ever-larger salary each year, the actual dollar amount of Company B's raise keeps growing, while Company A's raise stays fixed at exactly 2,000 dollars. Continuing the same calculation out to year 12, Company A pays exactly 64,000 dollars, while Company B has grown to about 64,041 dollars, meaning Company B has just overtaken Company A, and it will keep paying more every year after that, by a growing margin.

This leads to a general principle worth remembering: no matter how small a constant percent growth rate is, as long as it is greater than zero, and no matter how large a constant linear increase is, the exponential model will always eventually overtake the linear model if you wait long enough, because multiplying compounds on itself while adding does not. That is exactly why exponential growth is often described as being "faster in the long run," even in situations, like this one, where it clearly starts out slower.
